text: Everything this chapter built — a cross-cloud link, shared DNS, an awareness of egress cost — still leaves one question unanswered: what happens when one of the two providers has a bad day? This lesson is about designing so that answer is 'the other one keeps working,' not 'the whole platform goes down.'

Azure and AWS are genuinely independent failure domains. They share no power, no networking fabric, no incident response team, so a regional Azure outage has no mechanism to take down an AWS region, and the reverse holds too. That independence is exactly why multi-cloud strategy treats redundancy as a real motivation for going multi-cloud at all. But independence is a property of the infrastructure, not of your application — a design that assumes both clouds either work or fail together gets none of that benefit, and can actively turn a single-provider outage into a platform-wide one.

Here's how that happens. A service in Azure calls an AWS dependency on every request with no timeout. The AWS side gets slow, not down — and every one of those calls now hangs instead of failing fast. Each hung call holds a connection and a thread open and waiting. Enough of them, and the Azure service runs out of capacity entirely, becoming unavailable too, purely because it never stopped waiting on a struggling dependency it had no business trusting that much.

Four patterns close that gap. Timeouts on every cross-cloud call, so a slow dependency fails fast instead of hanging. Circuit breakers, which stop calling a dependency after enough consecutive failures instead of piling up more failing calls. Health-check-driven failover, routing traffic to whichever provider's path is actually healthy right now. And graceful degradation — deciding in advance what a service does when its cross-cloud dependency is unreachable, like serving a cached value, instead of failing the whole request.

This is the same principle Lesson 17 ended on, one layer up: a VPN configured as failover for a dedicated circuit works because two independent paths, not either one alone, make a connection resilient. Two independent cloud providers work the same way for an entire application — but only if the application is actually built to notice one side failing and keep functioning on the other, instead of assuming both always succeed or fail together.
